transcript: Going into this play, I knew that it was based on a true story about a son who turns his father in for participating in the January 6th insurrection. However, what I did not realize going in is that it was actually a verbatim play, meaning that every word of dialogue spoken in the show is coming directly from court documents for this particular case. And I thought that this was a really risky choice, because court cases, as you know, are famously boring, and how do you make an interesting and compelling narrative out of that? And I'm happy to report that those fears were completely unfounded in this case, because Fatherland manages to be incredibly tense and gripping in a way that I didn't expect it to be. And the fact that it is a verbatim text, knowing that all of the words said in this play actually were said, that's this layer of rawness to it that I don't think you'd be able to get otherwise. These characters feel so real and fleshed out because they are real and fleshed out. And even though all of the dialogue is taken directly from court documents, they do a good job at not keeping the whole thing in the courtroom the whole time. A lot of the scenes as they're telling the story will flash back to that moment in time. And so you're essentially just watching the events play out in chronological order, with the courtroom as a framing Device. And it's all integrated very seamlessly. I don't think I would even know that it was a verbatim play if they didn't tell you at the top of the show. They have to shout out the sound designed by Stuart Blackwood. It brings so many of these scenes to life, especially the scene where we see the father storm the capital. There really is not much set to this production, so the sound design goes a long way into pulling you in and making you feel immersed in some of these scenes. Overall, I think this is a really excellent case study and how effective verbatim theater can be, especially when used correctly. And while I was initially worried that the subject matter might be a little bit too soon, I really do think that this is a gripping look into the harsh realities of losing a loved one to political extremism. So definitely check it out at New York City Center Stage 2 if you are able to. It is running through November 23rd.
